 To build a sustainable launch stack that actually compounds over time, it helps to understand what each major platform brings to the table:
 1. Weekly Launch and SEO Equity: Platforms like LaunchOnIt fix the 24-hour burnout by giving products a full week on the leaderboard. This provides steady community interaction, real feedback, and permanent dofollow backlinks that compound your domain authority for search engines and AI answer engines.

 The ultimate guide to AI search optimization: how to get your SaaS cited by ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity 
If you have looked at your organic traffic channels over the last few months, you probably noticed a massive shift. More and more potential software buyers are skipping traditional Google search results pages entirely and instead asking conversational AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity for direct recommendations.
 When a user asks an AI tool for the best analytics software or the top productivity tool, the model does not give them ten blue links. It outputs a curated shortlist of three to five brands. If your startup is on that list, you capture high-converting intent. If you are not, you are completely invisible.
 This fundamental shift has given rise to new optimization frameworks: AEO (Answer Engine Optimization) and GEO (Generative Engine Optimization).
 Unlike traditional SEO, which focuses purely on keyword density and search rankings, AI search optimization is built around machine citation authority . Large Language Models do not just rank pages; they synthesize information from trusted third-party networks, structured directories, and entity mentions, then extract those sources directly into their answers.
 What actually moves the needle for AI citations? 
 1. Structured Entity Clarity: LLMs rely heavily on structured data, clean directory ecosystems, and consistent brand mentions across platforms like GitHub, Indie Hackers, and specialized curation boards to understand what your software actually does.
 2. Contextual Third-Party Proof: AI models validate your software by looking at how often you are cited alongside competitors in comparisons, alternative lists, and developer docs.
 3. Answer-First Formatting: Pages structured with concise, direct explanations immediately following headings perform significantly better because scrapers and AI retrieval agents can extract them without friction.
 While building tools like LaunchOnIt and monitoring brand footprints, it became obvious that distribution is no longer just about human clicks. It is about planting the digital footprints that AI agents look for when mapping out software categories.

 Building LaunchOnIt forced me to learn this the hard way. The moment we stopped trying to be a general marketplace for the entire internet and locked in strictly on bootstrapped indie hackers and solo founders who hate the daily launch grind, everything clicked.

 Building a business on rented land means you are constantly running on a treadmill just to stay in the same place.

 If you hit the front page, you get a massive surge of dopamine and traffic. If your launch gets buried by the algorithm or bad timing, your product disappears into the archive by Wednesday afternoon.

 The single point of failure that kills most indie SaaS startups within six months

 Either they get all their users from a lucky post on a specific social platform, or they spent three months optimizing for a single 24-hour launch day and expected the momentum to carry them forever. When that one tap dries up, panic sets in because there is no safety net.
 Building a resilient indie SaaS means treating distribution like a portfolio. You need multiple layers working together simultaneously. 
 That is why while building LaunchOnIt , I obsessed over baking multiple distribution loops right into the foundation. It is not just about showing up for a week. It is about combining community visibility, structured directory syndication, and long-term organic SEO footprint so that traffic compounds instead of flatlining.
 If your main traffic source vanished tomorrow morning, would your startup survive the week, or would your signups drop straight to absolute zero? How diversified is your distribution stack right now?

 The hidden cost of building features that users never actually touch

 I caught myself doing this recently while looking at the backend code for LaunchOnIt . They just wanted to submit their product, get their 7-day runway, and move on.

 The moment I stripped away the clutter and made the core submission flow dead simple, everything improved. The page loaded faster, support questions dropped to almost zero, and the conversion rate ticked up. 
 We forget that every extra feature we add is not just code we have to maintain, it is extra cognitive load we are forcing onto our users.

 I missed nothing in the LLM wave. I’m not missing the robot one. 
Two years ago I shipped FakeChatGPT.com . It’s a silly little tool that makes ChatGPT conversations that look real. People used it for memes, pranks and marketing mockups. It got [X] users and [X] visits a month, and it paid for itself from day one.
 It also taught me the most important lesson of my career:
 The money follows the wave, and the best time to get on it is before everyone sees it. 
 I was early to the LLM wave only because I was playing with it. Fake chats were a joke, but behind the joke I was watching a technology go from “neat demo” to thousends of users in about 18 months.
 So I started asking a different question: what’s the next ChatGPT moment, and where are the shovels? 
 My answer: robots. 
 The moment no one’s talking about (yet)
 Physical AI is where LLMs were in 2021. Foundation models for robots are improving every month. Humanoids are walking out of labs and into warehouses and supermarkets. Billions are flowing in.
 But the industry has a dirty secret: nobody can test their robots properly. 
 When you train a new robot policy, how do you know it’s better than the last one? Today the answer is usually “we ran it on the real robot a few times and it looked okay.” Picture shipping software with no tests, where every test costs an hour of hardware time and might break a $100k arm.
 LLMs got benchmarks, evals and leaderboards. Robots got vibes.
 So I built Hyperverse
 Hyperverse.sh is CI/CD for robot brains.
 📸 Real places become test arenas. We scan real spaces (a supermarket, an office, a family home) into photorealistic 3D worlds.
🤖 Every checkpoint gets scored. Point Hyperverse at a policy and it runs your benchmark suites in those arenas, then tells you if you got better or worse.
🔁 It runs on every training run, automatically. Like GitHub Actions, but for robots.
The jump from a meme generator to physics simulation and gaussian splats sounds huge. It wasn’t. The playbook was the same:
 Find the wave early
Build the boring, necessary tool everyone will need
Ship ugly, ship fast, talk to users
The tech changed. The instinct didn’t.
 Why I’m telling you this now
 Every gold rush has a window. For LLM wrappers it closed fast. In 2023 you could launch a GPT tool on a weekend and make $10k a month. By 2024 the space was packed.
 Physical AI is in that 2022 window right now. The tools aren’t built yet. The incumbents don’t exist yet. The indie hackers who move first will own categories.

 I built an alert system for 20+ equity crowdfunding platforms in three weeks of evenings 
In September I started a new job, and I’m also finishing an MSc. A week into the new job I started a side project. A sensible person probably wouldn’t have done it in that order.
 The itch
 In 2016, Revolut raised on Crowdcube at $2.14 a share. In 2024, those early backers were offered about $865. Anyone with £10 and an afternoon could have been one of them.
 When I started reading about equity crowdfunding, the upside wasn’t what struck me (there are plenty of horror stories too, more on those below). What struck me was how scattered it all is. In the US there’s Wefunder, Republic and StartEngine. The UK has Crowdcube. Europe has a dozen platforms, each in its own language. Australia has Birchal and Canada has FrontFundr. Every one of them wants you to make an account and keep checking back. Raises open and close within weeks, so if you weren’t watching the right site that week, you’d never know the deal existed.
 I looked for something that pulls all of this into one place. The US has some tools, but I couldn’t find a live campaign feed for Europe or the rest of the world. So I fell back on the old engineer reflex.
 Checking it wasn’t a dumb idea
 Before writing any code, I spent a weekend on feasibility. A few things surprised me:
 The whole global market is small. There are about 2,500 startup campaigns a year, roughly 10 a day. That’s a tractable data problem, not a big-data one.
The US hands you a free government feed. Every Reg CF raise has to file a Form C with the SEC, usually a few days before the campaign goes live, and EDGAR serves it as structured data. So US coverage of new raises was close to complete on day one.
Europe has nothing like that. The regulation requires an info sheet for each offer, but nobody publishes those centrally. You either scrape or partner.
Most European platforms serve plain HTML. A few US ones are JavaScript shells or sit behind bot protection.
That was good enough to start.
 The build
 I picked the boring stack I use every day: Nest.js, React and Postgres, running as one Docker container on Railway. I even copied the database tooling from another side project verbatim, so the same commands work in both. When you only have evenings, familiarity is a feature. Serverless was tempting, but some platforms need a real headless browser, and running Playwright in a long-running container with a stable IP is far less painful.
 Each platform gets its own adapter class. Today there are 23 sources: SEC EDGAR plus platforms in 15+ countries.
 The part I’m proudest of is unglamorous. The classic failure is a scraper that breaks silently: the site gets a redesign, the selector matches nothing, the adapter returns an empty list, the poll logs “success”, and nobody notices for six weeks. To guard against that:
 Adapters throw instead of returning empty.
Every run records what it saw.
A health check flags any source that hasn’t produced a new campaign in N days.
Uptime monitoring points at that check, not just at “is the server up”. Years of on-call make you paranoid in useful ways.
 The outbound side gets the same care. Every alert has a dedupe key, so a retry never sends you “closes in 72 hours” twice. When the whole promise of the product is timing, double emails would kill trust fast.
 The unsexy stuff that ate the most time
 Naming. It started as Rise Radar, but every domain variant was taken. My rule was a free .com for under $20, which turned out to be a real constraint. It’s now Raise Sonar.
Selling from Bulgaria to UK, EU and US consumers means VAT in a lot of places. I didn’t want to become a tax expert, so I went with a merchant-of-record setup.
Timezones. The entire product boils down to “this raise closes at time T” across a dozen jurisdictions. Every timestamp carries its timezone, no exceptions.
Risk warnings and legal pages for three different regulatory regimes. Not fun, but very necessary.
What it actually does
 Raise Sonar watches 20+ platforms and every SEC Form C filing. It emails you:
 when a raise matching your rules launches
7 days, 72 hours and 24 hours before it closes
when it reaches 90% of its cap, since those raises can close early
before an early-bird perk runs out
Rules read like plain sentences, e.g. “EU + UK · SaaS, Fintech · min ticket ≤ €500” . Tell it where you live and it badges which deals you can actually invest in.
 There’s a free weekly digest. Real-time alerts cost $10 a month, and a Pro tier adds the numbers behind each raise.
 The thing I didn’t expect to put on my homepage
 While researching, I found the outcome data sobering:
 Only about 6% of UK crowdfunded companies have ever exited, and about 20% went bust.
Nearly half of US crowdfunded companies don’t file the annual reports they’re required to.
BrewDog’s crowd investors were once shown a 2,765% paper gain and got nothing when the business sold.
I put all of that on the homepage, right under the Revolut story. It felt strange for a marketing page. But a product that only shows the winners is selling lottery tickets, and I’d rather people trust the alerts. Raise Sonar doesn’t give advice or pick deals. It makes sure you see them in time to decide for yourself.
 Where it is now
 It’s just launched. Next on the list:
 an AI write-up for every raise (valuation against comparable rounds, dilution, runway), with every line linked to its source
more platforms
Telegram and WhatsApp alerts
What I’d love from you
 If you invest in crowdfunding: what would make alerts worth paying for?
If you’ve grown a niche paid newsletter or alert product: where did your first 100 subscribers come from?
Roast the landing page: raisesonar.com

 What I learned testing a calendar sync tool against real-world setups 
I'm building Kelbra, which keeps calendars in sync across Google, Outlook, iCloud and CalDAV. Before writing any marketing, I tested it against the setups people complain about in forums. Some of it went fine, and some of it broke in ways I'm glad I found before users did.
 The setups people actually struggle with:
 People with calendars from different organizations: two part-time jobs, a consultant with a client-issued Outlook account, a work and a personal calendar. Each calendar only knows its own meetings.
 Microsoft Bookings users. Bookings only checks your default Outlook calendar, so a Google event or a second account doesn't block the slot. Microsoft's own moderators call it a known limitation.
 People who built the sync themselves in Zapier, Make or Power Automate, and now have duplicates, two automations triggering each other, and deletions that never reach the other calendar.
 What broke in my own testing:
 A "Busy only" mode (show other calendars only that you're busy, never the details) worked on the first sync, but editing the event later raised a false conflict, and resolving that conflict could have leaked the private details or overwritten the real event with "Busy". Fixed.
 Outlook connections silently died an hour after connecting, because the access token was never refreshed. Fixed.
 A weekly meeting with no end date expanded into every Monday until 2040, and the tool tried to create 730 events in one go. It now only syncs a year ahead.
 I turned what I learned into a few guides, each with the do-it-yourself fix first:
 https://www.getkelbra.com/guides 
 Two questions for anyone here: if you use more than one calendar, how do you keep them in step today? And if you've tried a sync tool before, what made you stop using it?

 My Show HN was killed on submit 
I've spent the last two years, on and off, building Alesian Security. Last Friday, I posted it as a ShowHN, and it never went live. It didn't fail, it never got a chance to.
 Alesian Security watches for lookalike domains (eg. yourcompany.co, y0urcompany.com, yourcompany-billing.com) that are or registered or have a change in disposition, evaluates the risk posed, and provides a path to have the risky domains blocked. I got into this having watched various paths that attackers used to perform Business Email Compromise and was tired of watching people get screwed.
 When I shared my project on Hacker News my post looked live, but I didn't see a comment field. Looking from a logged out window revealed that my post wasn't displaying and I emailed mods asking for help. So far I've not receive a response, my best guess is that a new domain tripped the spam filter. 
 I don't think the opportunity on Hacker News is over, but I think my product requires some retooling (and repackaging) to give it another shot. The Hacker News FAQ says:
 If a story has not had significant attention in the last year or so, a small number of reposts is ok. Otherwise we bury reposts as duplicates.
 Please don't delete and repost the same story. Deletion is for things that shouldn't have been submitted in the first place.
 IMO it's fair to say that it just isn't the launch I hoped for.
 Right now I'm sharing my experience (building in public) here on Indie Hackers, commenting in relevant subreddits, working my own network, and basic SEO.
 I still have no accounts created on the site and I haven't observed much in the way of use. Time will tell which of these avenues will have been most success. 
 Has anybody else had a launch quietly die like this? 
 What actually brought your first ten users?
